newsitem.title: UK: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON ALLOWED TO DEFEND WORLD TITLE.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-JOHNSON ALLOWED TO DEFEND WORLD TITLE.

text.p: Double Olympic champion Michael Johnson will be allowed to compete at next month's world athletics championships in Athens despite not being selected for the U.S. team.
The International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) announced on Monday that it would be giving wild cards to defending champions for the first time at the championships.

Johnson, who completed historic 200 and 400 metres doubles at both the last world championships and at last year's Atlanta Olympics, was not selected for the U.S. team after he missed the national trials because of injury.
But like compatriots such as hurdler Gail Devers, sprinter Gwen Torrence and decathlete Dan O'Brien, who all missed or failed to finish the trials, he now has the go-ahead to compete.
Brad Hunt, the agent of Johnson, Torrence and O'Brien immediately confirmed that the trio would compete in Athens.
The wild cards will also be given to champions at all world championships in the future including indoor and cross-country championships.
If their national teams agree, defending champions will also be allowed to switch events. Devers, for example, could compete in the 100 metres in Athens if the United States agreed.
The ruling largely affects the United States which has strict rules on qualification for major championships, allowing only the top three in the national trials to make the team.
The decision will certainly make their team much stronger and weaken the importance of the U.S. trials in the future.
It could also influence Kenyan and British athletes.

Britain's world triple jump champion Jonathan Edwards, who has been suffering with a heel injury, is now guaranteed his place at the event and does not need to prove his fitness to national selectors.
There was some opposition within the IAAF and among athletes to the move which is believed to have had the full backing of president Primo Nebiolo.
But the body's ruling council was persuaded that it was a decision which would help the promotion of the championships which take place every two years.

Johnson, who is presently training in Texas after being injured in his 150-metre showdown with Canadian world 100 metres record holder Donovan Bailey earlier in the season, is planning to come to the world championships "to do something very special." Hunt said.
Hunt praised Nebiolo for pushing for the ruling.
"You have to give him a lot of credit," Hunt said. "He does understand how to present the sport so that it is seen and followed by as many people as possible.

"The world championships were conceived 15 years ago to market the sport. I think this is a continuing development. Other sports certainly recognise their defending and former champions in similar ways."
